name: device-lifecycle
context: An IoT or edge fleet must be enrolled, authenticated, grouped, described, found and retired as a population rather than device by device. The registry holds an entry per physical thing — name, attributes, type, group membership — and provisioning is a template-driven act that mints the thing, the client certificate and the IoT policy together, so a device that joins the fleet becomes routable and authorised in one step instead of three manual ones. Grouping then becomes the unit at which policy, targeting and bulk operations apply.
benefits: Devices are provisioned from a versioned template, so onboarding a thousand units is a loop over parameter sets rather than a thousand console operations
Thing, certificate and policy are created together, removing the window where a device exists but cannot talk or can talk but is not registered
Provisioning by claim lets a device bootstrap itself on first connect using a shared claim certificate, then receive its own credentials
Thing groups form a hierarchy with inherited policies, so permission changes apply to a whole population in one edit
Dynamic groups express membership as a live query over connectivity, shadow existence and Device Defender findings, so the fleet stays classified without manual curation
tradeoffs: Registry state drifts from physical reality — a decommissioned device is indistinguishable from an offline one until the inventory is reconciled
Dynamic groups are eventually consistent: creation moves through a BUILDING state and membership changes lag the underlying facts
A group can have at most one direct parent and a thing belongs to at most ten groups, which constrains hierarchy design
Template parameters and override settings make provisioning subtly order-dependent; a re-provision can MERGE, REPLACE or leave attributes untouched depending on configuration
Certificate rotation at fleet scale requires group-level policy attachment rather than per-device edits, which couples security operations to the group model
use_cases: Onboarding a manufactured batch where serial numbers are known at packing time
Self-provisioning field devices that carry only a shared claim certificate
Rolling certificate rotation across an entire device group
Classifying a fleet by behaviour — devices that never connect, devices with no shadow, devices with Defender findings
Attaching and detaching authorisation policy across a fleet by group membership instead of per device
avoid_when: The deployment has a handful of devices — the registry machinery has real operational cost for no benefit
Devices are never re-provisioned, re-certified or decommissioned, so there is no lifecycle to manage
Identity is derived from a gateway rather than per device, making per-device registry entries redundant
The registry must be the authoritative real-time state of a device, which it is not — the shadow and the device are
component_types: Device registry: one record per thing with name, attributes, type and group memberships
Provisioning template: versioned parameterised declaration of thing, certificate and policy resources
Claim certificate: shared fleet credential used once for self-registration
Client certificate: per-device credential issued at provisioning and rotated independently
IoT policy: permission document attached to certificates or groups, inherited down the hierarchy
Static and dynamic thing groups: explicit membership versus membership derived from a registry query
technology_stack: AWS IoT provisioning templates and fleet provisioning
Azure IoT Hub device provisioning service
anti_patterns: Creating the thing, the certificate and the policy as separate manual steps per device, leaving partially onboarded devices
Using a per-device certificate embedded at manufacture, making rotation impossible without physical access
Ignoring group hierarchy constraints (one direct parent, ten groups per thing) and producing a model that cannot be expressed
Treating dynamic group membership as immediately consistent and acting on it before the BUILDING backfill completes
Using the registry as the source of truth for device state instead of the device shadow
design_principles: Registry, identity and authorisation are provisioned atomically as one template
Per-device credentials are the default; shared claim credentials are a bootstrap, not a steady state
Grouping is the unit of fleet-scale policy and targeting
Dynamic membership expresses intent as a query, not as curated state
The registry describes identity and grouping; it does not describe live device state
best_practices: Version provisioning templates and pin devices to a version so a fleet rollout is reproducible
Use group-attached policies so a certificate rotation is one group edit rather than N device edits
Plan the group hierarchy before creating children — a group's parent cannot be changed later
Treat dynamic group membership as eventually consistent and gate automation on the ACTIVE status
Keep claim certificates out of steady state; rotate provisioned devices onto their own credentials
references: AWS IoT, Provisioning templates — JITP, bulk registration and fleet provisioning, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot/latest/developerguide/provision-template.html
AWS IoT, Device provisioning — provisioning by claim and resource creation, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot/latest/developerguide/iot-provision.html
AWS IoT, Thing groups — hierarchies, policy inheritance and membership limits, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot/latest/developerguide/thing-groups.html
AWS IoT, Dynamic thing groups — membership from registry queries and the BUILDING backfill state, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot/latest/developerguide/dynamic-thing-groups.html
